lessons.title: Study Session 1: Organizing a Growing Queue of Orders

blocks.text: Organizing a Growing Queue of Orders Introduction Aïcha Ouédraogo sells wax-print fabric and traditional dress from Koudougou, and tracked orders only in her head and in scattered notes across her phone, working through requests in whatever order she happened to notice them rather than the order they were placed, until a customer who paid first ended up waiting three weeks while several orders placed after hers were finished and delivered ahead of it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about managing backlog variation in order fulfillment. Distinguish an order queue with no visible priority from one organized by a real rule. Apply a method for organizing and prioritizing a growing queue of orders. Recognise the signs that an order queue has outgrown informal tracking. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Customer Who Paid First but Waited Longest Aïcha Ouédraogo tracked orders only in her head and in scattered notes across her phone, working through requests in whatever order she happened to notice them rather than the order they were placed. A customer who paid for a custom dress before anyone else that week ended up waiting three weeks for it, while several orders placed after hers were finished and delivered first, simply because they had stayed more visible in Aïcha's messages. 2.2 What Research Found About Backlog Variation in Order Fulfillment Tingting Yan, Elliot Rabinovich, Kevin Dooley and Philip T. Evers studied how internet retailers could manage variation in their order backlog for a 2010 study. Rules that released inventory and prioritized orders by due date were found to produce the highest fill rate and the most reliable timeliness, and in most cases the lowest total cost, compared to less structured approaches to working through a backlog. 2.3 Organizing a Queue Around a Real Rule Recording Every Order the Moment It Arrives Logging every order onto one master list as soon as it comes in, with its date and any promised delivery time noted beside it, replaces memory and scattered messages with a single place that shows every order's actual place in line. Working the Queue by Due Date, Not by Visibility Working through the list by due date, oldest promised delivery first, rather than by whichever order happens to be easiest to see in the moment, keeps the order that has waited longest from being the one that waits longest again. 2.4 Key Practices Log every order onto one master list as soon as it comes in. Work the queue by due date, not by which order is easiest to see. Note a promised delivery date for every order, not just some. Review the full list at the start of each working day. 2.5 A Worked Example: Aïcha's Rebuilt Queue Aïcha built one master list of every order, logging each one's date and promised delivery window as soon as it came in, and began working through the list strictly by due date rather than by whichever message happened to be most recent. Aïcha's dressmaking itself had never caused a single one of her delays, and every piece she finished met the standard her customers expected. Nothing in her list told her which order had actually waited longest until she built one, and only working the queue by due date ever gave her earliest customer the place in line that customer's payment had already earned. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Tracking orders only in memory or scattered messages, with no single list showing each order's real place in line, lets an early paying customer disappear behind orders that simply stayed more visible, exactly what happened to Aïcha. Working through a queue by whichever order is easiest to see rather than by due date rewards visibility over fairness and lets the oldest order wait longest. 2.7 The Order That Waited Longest Should Not Wait Again The customers who kept returning to Aïcha never once doubted her fabric or her stitching. What her business lacked was any single place recording which order had actually been waiting longest, and only a real due-date rule ever gave her first customer the place in line that customer had earned by paying first. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to organize a growing queue of orders around a real due-date rule rather than memory or visibility. Study Session 2 turns from organizing the orders themselves to choosing who actually carries them to the customer. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about how you currently track orders. Would you be able to tell, at a glance, which order has been waiting the longest? 2. Build one master list of every current order for one real small business, recording each one's date and promised delivery window. 6.0 Practical Output A master order list for one real small business, recording every current order's date and promised delivery window, organized by due date. 7.0 References and Further Reading Yan, T., Rabinovich, E., Dooley, K., & Evers, P.T. (2010). Managing backlog variation in order fulfillment: The case of Internet retailers. International Journal of Production Economics, 128(1), 261 to 268. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Genesis 41:34, on appointing officers over the land and taking up the fifth part in the years of plenty. Qur'an, Surah An-Naml 27:39, on the one who said, I will bring it to you before you rise from your place.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Choosing and Working with Delivery and Courier Partners

blocks.text: Choosing and Working with Delivery and Courier Partners Introduction Semhar Tesfaye rebuilt her woven basket and handicraft business in Adigrat after being displaced from a neighbouring conflict area, and chose whichever courier quoted the lowest price for each individual delivery, until a single courier lost three of her packages within one month with no way to trace them and no compensation offered, and she realized she had never actually compared that courier's reliability against any other before trusting it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about selecting a logistics service provider for e-commerce businesses. Distinguish choosing a delivery partner purely by price from choosing one against a real set of criteria. Apply a method for evaluating and working with delivery and courier partners. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Three Lost Packages and No One to Ask Semhar Tesfaye chose whichever courier quoted the lowest price for each individual delivery, switching between several with no record of how reliably any of them had actually performed. One courier lost three of her packages within a single month, offered no way to trace them and no compensation, and Semhar realized she had never actually compared that courier's reliability against any other before trusting it with her customers' orders. 2.2 What Research Found About Selecting a Logistics Service Provider Muhammad Hamza Naseem, Jiaqi Yang and Ziquan Xiang studied how e-commerce companies could select a logistics service provider for a 2021 study of a business in Faisalabad, Pakistan. A structured evaluation across seven criteria, including reliability and cost, produced a different and better-fitted choice of provider than an unstructured comparison based on a single factor such as price alone. 2.3 Evaluating a Delivery Partner Against Real Criteria Setting a Small Set of Criteria Before Comparing Any Courier Deciding in advance on a small set of criteria, reliability, cost, coverage area and how losses are handled, before comparing any courier against another, keeps the choice from defaulting to whichever quote looks cheapest in the moment. Tracking Each Courier's Actual Performance Over Time Keeping a simple record of how each courier actually performed, on-time deliveries, losses, damaged items, over weeks and months, turns a first impression into evidence a business can act on the next time a delivery is booked. 2.4 Key Practices Decide on a small set of criteria before comparing any courier. Keep a simple record of each courier's actual performance over time. Ask directly how a courier handles a lost or damaged package before relying on them. 2.5 A Worked Example: Semhar's Evaluated Couriers Semhar set four criteria, reliability, cost, coverage of her customers' areas and how losses were handled, and began tracking every delivery against the courier that carried it, dropping the courier that had lost her packages once its record over several weeks made the pattern impossible to miss. Semhar's baskets and handicrafts had never been the reason a customer went without an order; every item she shipped left her hands complete and well packed. No record existed anywhere showing which courier actually lost packages and which one did not, and only tracking that performance over time ever let her see the pattern in time to act on it. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Choosing a courier by price alone, with no criteria for reliability or how losses are handled, leaves a business exposed to exactly the pattern that cost Semhar three packages in a single month. Switching couriers without keeping any record of past performance means a business relearns the same lesson with a new provider instead of building real evidence over time. 2.7 The Cheapest Courier Is Not Always the One Carrying the Least Risk Semhar's handicrafts had built a loyal customer base well before the lost packages began. The courier carrying them had never been evaluated against any real standard, and only setting criteria and tracking performance over time ever showed her which courier was actually worth trusting with an order. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to evaluate and work with delivery and courier partners against real criteria rather than price alone. Study Session 3 turns from choosing who delivers an order to promising, and keeping, a delivery window customers can rely on. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about how you currently choose a delivery partner. Is the choice based on real criteria, or mainly on price? 2. Set a small list of criteria for evaluating a delivery or courier partner for one real small business, and begin recording their actual performance. 6.0 Practical Output A set of courier evaluation criteria and a simple performance record for one real small business, tracking at least one delivery partner's reliability over time. 7.0 References and Further Reading Naseem, M.H., Yang, J., & Xiang, Z. (2021). Selection of logistics service provider for the e-commerce companies in Pakistan based on integrated GRA-TOPSIS approach. Axioms, 10(3), Article 208. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 2 Corinthians 8:23, on Titus being a partner and fellow helper. Qur'an, Surah Al-Qasas 28:26, on the best one to hire being the one who is strong and trustworthy.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Setting Delivery Windows the Business Can Actually Keep

blocks.text: Setting Delivery Windows the Business Can Actually Keep Introduction Kwame Osei sells handcrafted wooden furniture from Nkawkaw, and told every customer their order would arrive within a few days regardless of how many other orders were already ahead of theirs in his workshop, until a customer who ordered a dining table was told a week and waited three, because Kwame had quoted the same optimistic window to everyone that month without checking whether his workshop's actual schedule could support it. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the effect of delivery time on repurchase behaviour. Distinguish a delivery window based on optimism from one based on actual capacity. Apply a method for setting delivery windows the business can actually keep. Recognise when a delivery promise needs to be adjusted before it is made, not after. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Same Promise Made to Everyone Kwame Osei told every customer their furniture would arrive within a few days, regardless of how many other orders were already ahead of theirs in his workshop. A customer who ordered a dining table was told a week; three weeks later the table finally arrived, because Kwame had quoted the same optimistic window to every customer that month without checking whether his workshop's actual schedule could support it. 2.2 What Research Found About Delivery Time and Repurchase Behaviour Alice Harter, Lucas Stich and Martin Spann examined how delivery time shaped repurchase behaviour in quick commerce for a 2025 study. Late deliveries were found to harm repurchase behaviour more strongly than early deliveries of the same size helped it, meaning the accuracy of a delivery promise mattered more to a returning customer than how fast that promise was in the first place. 2.3 Setting a Window Based on Real Capacity Checking the Actual Workload Before Quoting a Window Checking how many orders are already ahead of a new one, and how long each genuinely takes to finish, before quoting a delivery window, replaces a hopeful guess with a promise grounded in what the workshop can actually deliver that week. Building in Room for the Unexpected Adding a small buffer to a calculated delivery window, rather than quoting the fastest possible outcome, protects the promise from the ordinary delays, a delayed material delivery, a slow week, that a tightly calculated window leaves no room to absorb. 2.4 Key Practices Check the actual workload ahead of a new order before quoting a delivery window. Add a small buffer to a calculated window rather than quoting the fastest possible outcome. Quote a longer window to a customer placing an order during a busy period. Tell a customer as soon as a promised window will not be met, rather than after it has passed. 2.5 A Worked Example: Kwame's Recalculated Windows Kwame began checking his actual order backlog before quoting a delivery window to any new customer, adding several days of buffer to whatever his honest calculation produced, and started quoting longer windows during weeks when his workshop was already full. Kwame's woodworking itself had never been the source of a single late table; every piece he built met the standard his customers expected. The delivery window attached to that table had been guessed rather than calculated, and only checking his actual backlog before quoting ever gave a customer a promise his workshop could really keep. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Quoting the same optimistic delivery window to every customer, regardless of how full the workshop's schedule already is, sets a promise that only holds true when nothing else is happening, exactly what produced Kwame's three-week table. Waiting until a promised window has already passed to tell a customer it will be late turns a manageable delay into a broken promise discovered the hard way. 2.7 A Promise Kept Late Is Still a Promise Broken Kwame's furniture had a growing reputation for quality that the delivery delays never touched directly. The window attached to each piece had been set by hope rather than by his workshop's real capacity, and only calculating that window honestly ever let a promise made match a promise kept. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to set delivery windows the business can actually keep, based on real capacity rather than optimism. Study Session 4 turns from the promise made at the start of a delivery to keeping the customer informed while it is underway. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about how you currently quote a delivery window. Is it based on your actual workload, or on what sounds reasonable to say? 2. Calculate a real delivery window for one current order at a real small business, based on actual workload plus a buffer. 6.0 Practical Output A calculated delivery window for one current order at a real small business, based on actual workload ahead of it plus a buffer for the unexpected. 7.0 References and Further Reading Harter, A., Stich, L., & Spann, M. (2025). The effect of delivery time on repurchase behavior in quick commerce. Journal of Service Research, 28, 211 to 227. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Psalm 89:34, on not breaking a covenant, nor altering the thing that has gone out of one's lips. Qur'an, Surah Al-Baqarah 2:177, on fulfilling one's covenant when a covenant has been made.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit

blocks.text: Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit Introduction Boubacar Diallo sells phone accessories and small electronics from Kankan, and shipped an order and then gave the customer nothing further until it physically arrived, until one customer, unable to see where her order actually was, messaged him nine separate times over four days asking for a status update, each answered individually before Boubacar realized responding to all nine had cost him more time than an update sent at the start would have. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about how an express delivery promise shapes customer ratings. Distinguish silence between dispatch and delivery from proactive status updates. Apply a method for tracking delivery status and keeping customers informed in transit. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Nine Messages for One Package Boubacar Diallo shipped an order and then gave the customer nothing further until it physically arrived, with no tracking information and no update in between. One customer, unable to see where her order actually was, messaged Boubacar nine separate times over four days asking for a status update, and each message was answered individually before Boubacar realized responding to all nine had cost him more time than simply telling her where the order stood at the start would have. 2.2 What Research Found About Express Delivery Promises and Ratings Ali Ahmed, Amit Deokar, Hyung Cheol Brian Lee and Nick Summerfield examined how an express delivery promise shaped customer ratings on an e-commerce platform for a 2024 study. An express delivery promise was found to raise a customer's expectations enough that orders shipped under that promise received fewer and lower ratings than equivalent orders without it, even when the express order arrived on time or early. 2.3 Tracking Status and Communicating It Proactively Sharing Tracking Information the Moment an Order Ships Sharing tracking information, or a clear status update, the moment an order ships, rather than waiting for a customer to ask, gives the customer somewhere to look besides a message to the seller. Sending an Update at Each Real Change in Status Sending a short update whenever an order's status genuinely changes, dispatched, out for delivery, delivered, keeps a customer informed without requiring them to ask, and without sending updates that say nothing new. 2.4 Key Practices Share tracking information or a status update the moment an order ships. Send a short update at each real change in an order's status. Set expectations plainly about promised delivery speed, since a faster promise raises what a customer expects in return. 2.5 A Worked Example: Boubacar's Status Updates Boubacar began sending a short message the moment an order shipped, giving a tracking reference where available and an honest estimate of arrival, then sent one further update when an order reached its final stage before delivery, without waiting for a customer to ask first. Boubacar's shipping itself had rarely gone wrong; most orders arrived within the window he expected. Nothing told a customer where an order actually stood between dispatch and arrival until he built that habit, and only sending updates at real changes in status ever gave a customer a reason not to ask nine times. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Going silent between dispatch and delivery, with no tracking information and no update offered, pushes an anxious customer to ask repeatedly, exactly the pattern behind Boubacar's nine messages. Promising unusually fast delivery without communicating clearly raises a customer's expectations high enough that even an on-time delivery can land as a disappointment. 2.7 An Update Sent Once Is Cheaper Than Nine Questions Answered Boubacar's phone accessories rarely arrived late; the actual delivery performance behind his business was solid. What was missing was any information reaching the customer between the moment an order left his hands and the moment it arrived, and only proactive updates ever closed that gap. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to track delivery status and keep customers informed proactively while an order is in transit. Study Session 5 turns from keeping a customer informed to responding well when a delivery does not go as planned. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about your own delivery communication. Does a customer have to ask for a status update, or is one sent to them automatically? 2. Write a short shipment update and a short final-stage update for one real order, and send both without waiting for the customer to ask. 6.0 Practical Output A shipment update and a final-stage delivery update written for one real order, sent proactively without the customer having to ask. 7.0 References and Further Reading Ahmed, A., Deokar, A., Lee, H.C.B., & Summerfield, N. (2024). The role of commitment in online reputation systems: An empirical study of express delivery promise in an e-commerce platform. Decision Support Systems, 176, Article 114061. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Habakkuk 2:1, on standing upon the watch and watching to see what will be said. Qur'an, Surah Al-An'am 6:59, on not a leaf falling but that He knows it.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Handling Delivery Exceptions Without Losing the Customer

blocks.text: Handling Delivery Exceptions Without Losing the Customer Introduction Chiamaka Eze raises her two children alone while running her baby clothing and supplies business in Ihiala, and had no set process for what happened when a delivery failed, so when one order came back to her after three failed delivery attempts, no one told the customer why, and the customer, who had already paid, eventually posted publicly about never receiving an order she had no way of knowing had already failed and come back. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the effect of order fulfillment failures on future customer behaviour. Distinguish an unexplained delivery failure from one handled with a clear process. Apply a method for responding to delivery exceptions without losing the customer. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 An Order Returned With No Explanation Given Chiamaka Eze had no set process for what happened when a delivery failed, so when one customer's order came back to her after three failed delivery attempts, no one had told the customer why, and no one reached out to explain or offer a solution. The customer, who had already paid and was left simply waiting, eventually posted publicly about never receiving an order she had no way of knowing had already failed and come back. 2.2 What Research Found About Order Fulfillment Failures Pedro Amorim, Fredrik Eng-Larsson and Robert P. Rooderkerk examined how online order fulfillment failures shaped future customer behaviour for a 2025 study. How a retailer responded to a fulfillment failure was found to measurably shape whether the customer purchased again, independent of the failure itself, meaning the response mattered as much to the relationship as the original mistake. 2.3 Responding to a Delivery Exception With a Clear Process Reaching Out the Moment a Delivery Fails, Not After Reaching out to the customer the moment a delivery is confirmed to have failed, rather than waiting for the customer to notice and ask, turns a silent failure into a problem the business is visibly already handling. Offering a Clear Next Step, Not Just an Apology Offering a specific next step, a redelivery date, a refund, or a corrected address confirmed with the customer, rather than an apology alone, gives the customer something concrete instead of continued uncertainty about the same order. 2.4 Key Practices Reach out to the customer the moment a delivery is confirmed to have failed. Offer a specific next step, not just an apology, for every failed delivery. Record why each delivery failed to spot a pattern before it repeats. 2.5 A Worked Example: Chiamaka's Delivery Exception Process Chiamaka built a simple process for failed deliveries, contacting the customer the same day a failure was confirmed, explaining what had happened, and offering a redelivery or refund immediately rather than waiting for the customer to ask, and began recording the reason behind every failure to watch for a pattern. Chiamaka's baby products themselves had done nothing to cause a single failed delivery; every item she packed left in good condition and on schedule. The customer who never received her order had been left to wonder why with no one telling her, and only reaching out the moment a failure was confirmed ever replaced that silence with an answer. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Leaving a failed delivery unexplained, with no outreach until the customer notices and asks, allows frustration to build in the silence, exactly what turned Chiamaka's return into a public complaint. Offering only an apology for a failed delivery, without a specific next step attached, leaves the customer with the same uncertainty they started with. 2.7 How a Failure Is Handled Outlasts the Failure Itself Chiamaka's baby products had a loyal following among mothers in Ihiala who trusted her judgment. A single failed delivery, handled in silence, threatened that trust more than the failure itself did, and only a clear, prompt response ever protected the relationship the failure had put at risk. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to respond to delivery exceptions with a clear process rather than silence. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to how a growing business balances delivery cost, speed and reliability as its order volume increases. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about how a failed delivery is currently handled in your own business. Does the customer hear from you first, or do they have to ask? 2. Write a simple delivery exception process for one real small business, including what to say to a customer and what next step to offer. 6.0 Practical Output A written delivery exception process for one real small business, including a customer outreach step and a specific next step to offer for a failed delivery. 7.0 References and Further Reading Amorim, P., Eng-Larsson, F., & Rooderkerk, R.P. (2025). Navigating online order fulfillment failures: Impacts on future customer behavior and the role of retailer mitigation. Journal of Retailing, 101(3), 382 to 408. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Deuteronomy 24:19, on leaving the sheaf forgotten in the field for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow. Qur'an, Surah Ad-Duha 93:6, on did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Balancing Delivery Cost, Speed and Reliability as Order Volume Grows

blocks.text: Balancing Delivery Cost, Speed and Reliability as Order Volume Grows Introduction Naledi Mokoena sells stationery and office supplies from eMalahleni, and offered free next-day delivery on every order by default as her business grew, without ever calculating what that option actually cost her per order, until she finally worked out her real delivery cost months later and found that the fastest option she offered to everyone by default had been quietly consuming close to a third of her profit on every sale. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the trade-offs shaping online delivery design. Distinguish a delivery option chosen by default from one chosen deliberately against cost, speed and reliability. Apply a method for balancing delivery cost, speed and reliability as order volume grows. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 The Free Next-Day Delivery That Was Quietly Eating Her Profit Naledi Mokoena offered free next-day delivery on every order by default as her stationery and office supplies business grew, without ever calculating what that option actually cost her per order. Months later, once she finally worked out her real delivery cost, she found that the fastest option she offered to everyone by default had been quietly consuming close to a third of her profit on every single sale. 2.2 What Research Found About Trade-Offs in Delivery Design Reem Hadeed examined the trade-offs shaping online delivery options across UK retail and logistics for a 2026 study combining a literature review with an analysis of delivery offers published on retailer websites. Delivery design was found to be shaped overwhelmingly by speed, price visibility and convenience, with other genuine trade-offs, including cost to the business itself, rarely built into the actual point where a customer chose an option. 2.3 Choosing Delivery Options Deliberately Calculating the Real Cost of Every Delivery Option Offered Calculating the actual cost per order of every delivery option offered, rather than assuming a popular option is an affordable one, shows a business exactly what speed is costing it before that cost becomes a habit built into every sale. Offering a Deliberate Mix Instead of One Default Offering a small mix of delivery options, with clear pricing that reflects their real cost difference, rather than a single free fast default for every order, lets the customer's own choice help carry the cost that speed actually creates. 2.4 Key Practices Calculate the actual cost per order of every delivery option offered. Offer a small mix of delivery options with pricing that reflects their real cost difference. Revisit delivery pricing whenever order volume changes meaningfully. 2.5 A Worked Example: Naledi's Recalculated Delivery Options Naledi calculated the real per-order cost of next-day delivery against her standard delivery option, then introduced a small delivery fee on next-day orders while keeping standard delivery free, reflecting the actual cost difference between the two rather than absorbing it by default. Naledi's stationery business had grown for good reason; her products and her prices had both earned real customer loyalty. The next-day option she offered every customer by default had never been checked against what it actually cost her, and only calculating that cost ever showed her how much of her own profit a habit formed months earlier had been quietly spending. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Offering a single fast delivery option to every customer by default, without calculating its real cost, lets that option quietly consume profit the way it did for Naledi for months before anyone noticed. Assuming a delivery option is worth keeping simply because customers like it ignores whether the business can actually afford to keep offering it at a growing volume. 2.7 Speed a Business Cannot Afford Is Not Really a Service Naledi's business had grown because customers trusted her products and her prices, not because of a delivery speed she had never actually costed. A default chosen once, before volume grew large enough to matter, had kept costing her the same margin on every order since, and only recalculating that default ever gave her a delivery mix her growing business could actually sustain. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to balance delivery cost, speed and reliability deliberately as order volume grows. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Warehouse and Inventory Space Management for Small Enterprises, the next course in Pathway 63. 5.0 Self-Assessment Questions 1. Think about your own delivery options. Do you know the actual cost per order of each one, or is a default simply assumed to be affordable? 2. Calculate the real per-order cost of at least one delivery option for a real small business, and compare it against the price currently charged for it. 6.0 Practical Output A cost calculation comparing at least two delivery options for one real small business, with a recommendation for how each should be priced going forward. 7.0 References and Further Reading Hadeed, R. (2026). Speed or green? Strategic trade-offs in online delivery options across UK retail and logistics. Logistics, 10(6), Article 124. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 22:29, on a man diligent in his business standing before kings. Qur'an, Surah Al-Isra 17:30, on the Lord extending provision for whom He wills, and restricting it.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

quiz.q: A customer messaged Boubacar nine times over four days asking for a status update. What did this reveal?
options: Boubacar's phone accessories had stopped meeting quality expectations
Going silent between dispatch and delivery, with no tracking information offered, pushes an anxious customer to ask repeatedly
Phone accessories should not be sold with delivery included
Boubacar had been overpricing his products
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Ahmed, Deokar, Lee and Summerfield's 2024 study, what effect did an express delivery promise have on ratings?
options: Orders under an express promise received fewer and lower ratings, even when delivered on time or early
Express delivery always improved ratings regardless of outcome
Ratings were unaffected by any delivery promise
Express delivery promises only affected ratings for late orders
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit) before continuing.

quiz.q: An order returned to Chiamaka after three failed delivery attempts with no explanation given to the customer. What did this reveal?
options: Chiamaka's baby products had stopped meeting quality standards
Leaving a failed delivery unexplained, with no outreach until the customer notices, allows frustration to build in the silence
Baby products should not be shipped by delivery
Chiamaka had been overpricing her products
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Delivery Exceptions Without Losing the Customer) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Amorim, Eng-Larsson and Rooderkerk's 2025 study, what measurably shaped whether a customer purchased again after a fulfillment failure?
options: How the retailer responded to the failure, independent of the failure itself
Only the size of the refund offered
Nothing; repurchase behaviour was unaffected by the response
The customer's original order value
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Delivery Exceptions Without Losing the Customer) before continuing.

quiz.q: Naledi found that her free next-day delivery default had been consuming close to a third of her profit on every sale. What did this reveal?
options: Naledi's stationery products had stopped attracting genuine customers
Offering a single fast delivery option to every customer by default, without calculating its real cost, lets that option quietly consume profit
Free delivery should never be offered by a small business
Naledi had been pricing her stationery incorrectly
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 6 (Balancing Delivery Cost, Speed and Reliability as Order Volume Grows) before continuing.

quiz.q: According to Hadeed's 2026 study, what was found to shape online delivery design overwhelmingly?
options: Speed, price visibility and convenience, with cost to the business rarely built into the point of customer choice
Sustainability alone
Random variation with no consistent pattern
Only the size of the retailer offering the delivery
quiz.explain: Review Study Session 6 (Balancing Delivery Cost, Speed and Reliability as Order Volume Grows) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend recording the moment an order arrives?
options: Nothing; orders should be tracked from memory
The order onto one master list, with its date and any promised delivery time
Only orders above a certain value
A separate list for each customer
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Organizing a Growing Queue of Orders) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend deciding before comparing any courier?
options: Nothing; the cheapest courier should always be chosen
A small set of criteria, such as reliability, cost, coverage and loss handling
A single supplier for every future delivery
The courier's advertising budget
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Choosing and Working with Delivery and Courier Partners) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend checking before quoting a delivery window?
options: Nothing; a standard window should be quoted to every customer
The actual workload already ahead of the new order
Only the customer's location
The competitor's advertised delivery speed
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Setting Delivery Windows the Business Can Actually Keep) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend sharing the moment an order ships?
options: Nothing further until the order arrives
Tracking information or a clear status update
Only the seller's contact number
A discount code for the next purchase
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend doing the moment a delivery is confirmed to have failed?
options: Waiting for the customer to notice and ask
Reaching out to the customer immediately, rather than waiting
Cancelling the customer's account
Offering nothing until the next order is placed
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 5 (Handling Delivery Exceptions Without Losing the Customer) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What does this session recommend calculating for every delivery option offered?
options: Nothing; the most popular option should simply be kept
The actual cost per order of that delivery option
Only the customer's stated preference
The competitor's delivery pricing alone
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 6 (Balancing Delivery Cost, Speed and Reliability as Order Volume Grows) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What change did Aïcha make to her order tracking?
options: She stopped accepting new orders
She built one master list and worked it strictly by due date
She began working through orders by whichever was most recent
She removed dates from her order records
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 1 (Organizing a Growing Queue of Orders) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What change did Semhar make to how she chose couriers?
options: She stopped shipping to certain regions
She set criteria and began tracking each courier's actual performance over time
She switched to the most expensive courier available
She stopped offering delivery entirely
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 2 (Choosing and Working with Delivery and Courier Partners) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What change did Kwame make to how he quoted delivery windows?
options: He stopped quoting any delivery window at all
He checked his actual backlog and added a buffer before quoting a window
He quoted the same window regardless of his workshop's schedule
He removed delivery entirely and required customer pickup
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 3 (Setting Delivery Windows the Business Can Actually Keep) before continuing.

finalQuiz.q: What change did Boubacar make to his delivery communication?
options: He stopped responding to customer messages
He began sending a status update at shipment and at the order's final stage before delivery
He removed tracking information from all orders
He started charging extra for status updates
finalQuiz.explain: Review Study Session 4 (Tracking Delivery Status and Keeping Customers Informed in Transit) before continuing.
